content.text: {"relation":"MATCH","consensus_summary":"All three blind responses converge on the same primary reading: biblical 'knowing' (yada'/ginōskō) denotes intimate, experiential, covenantal relationship rather than mere intellectual awareness, with knowing God evidenced by obedience and love (1 John 2:3-4), the marital/sexual euphemism (Gen 4:1) as a standard sub-sense, and God's 'knowing' persons as covenantal recognition or election (Matt 7:23; Amos 3:2).","book_summary":"The book defines knowing as covenant relationship proven by obedience, explicitly invoking the intimate marital 'knew' (Gen 4:1) and the negative case that a 'stranger' is one not known (Matt 7:23), with 1 John 2:3-4 as the obedience test and Hos 4:6 on destruction for lack of knowledge.","rationale":"The book's entry combines the exact elements the consensus identifies as dominant: relational/covenantal knowledge, obedience as its evidence, and the marital-intimacy sense as an illustration of the same root idea. Every component of the book's formulation—covenant, obedience-proof, marital intimacy, exclusion of the un-known—appears in the blind responses' primary meaning or its acknowledged sub-senses (Responses A, B, and C all cite Gen 4:1, Matt 7:23, and 1 John 2:3-4 in support of the relational reading). Nothing in the entry contradicts or displaces the common interpretation; it is a compact restatement of it rather than a materially sharper or narrower claim.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue the entry is REFINED rather than MATCH because it foregrounds 'proven by obedience' as the defining criterion, making the 1 John test central where the consensus treats obedience as one evidence among several facets (love, communion, election); the book's fusion of the marital and covenantal senses into a single definition is slightly tighter than the consensus's list of distinct sub-senses.","confidence":"high"}
